metadata.title: A generalization of the Gauss-Bonnet and Hopf-Poincaré theorems
metadata.authors: F. A. Arias and M. Malakhaltsev

nodes.name: Hopf-Poincaré theorem
nodes.statement: The classical Hopf-Poincaré theorem affirms that the sum of indices of zeros of $V$ is equal to the Euler characteristic of $M$: \begin{equation} \sum_{z \in Z(V)} ind_{z}(V) = \chi(M), \end{equation} where $Z(V)$ is the set of zeros of $V$ and $ind_{z}(V)$ is the index of $V$ at $z$ (see for example~\cite{bott_tu1982}).
nodes.statement_short: The sum of the indices of the zeros of a vector field on a closed oriented surface equals $\chi(M)$.
assumptions: Let $M$ be a $2$-dimensional compact oriented manifold, and $V$ be a vector field on $M$.
conclusions: \sum_{z \in Z(V)} ind_{z}(V) = \chi(M)

nodes.name: Gauss-Bonnet theorem
nodes.statement: If, in addition, the manifold $M$ is endowed by a Riemannian metric $g$, then the Gauss-Bonnet theorem says that the Euler characteristic is expressed in terms of the curvature $K$ of this metric: \begin{equation} \chi(M) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_M K d\sigma, \end{equation} where $d\sigma$ is the area form of $g$.
nodes.statement_short: The Euler characteristic of a closed Riemannian surface is the normalized total curvature.
assumptions: the manifold $M$ is endowed by a Riemannian metric $g$
conclusions: \chi(M) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_M K d\sigma

nodes.name: Classical Hopf-Poincaré-Gauss-Bonnet formula
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \sum_{z \in Z(V)} ind_{z}(V) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_M K d\sigma, \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Total curvature equals the sum of the indices of the zeros of a vector field.

Then for any $x \in \Sigma$, there exist one and only one boundary component $\partial S_i$ such that $\pi^{-1}(x) = q(\partial S_i)$. \emph{e)} For any $x \in \Sigma$ exists a neighborhood $U$ of $x$ such that \begin{enumerate} \item $U$ is diffeomorphic to a disk; \item There exists a closed set $V \subset S$ diffeomorphic to a ring such that the boundary of $V$ consists of two connected components $C$ and $C'$, where the connected component $C$ is a closed curve in $S \setminus \partial S$ and the other connected component $C'$ is the connected component $\partial S_i$ of the boundary $\partial S$ which corresponds to $x$ by d), and \begin{equation} \pi \circ q(C) = \partial U, \quad \pi \circ q(V \setminus \partial V) = U \setminus x, \quad \pi \circ q(\partial S_i) = x \end{equation} \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Proof of the structure theorem for resolutions
nodes.statement: a) $s : M \setminus \Sigma \to s(M \setminus \Sigma)$ is a diffeomorphism and $\left. \pi \right|_{s(M \setminus \Sigma)} : s(M \setminus \Sigma) \to M \setminus \Sigma$ is the diffeomorphism inverse to $s$. Therefore $\pi \circ q : S \setminus \partial S \to M \setminus \Sigma$ is a diffeomorphism b) For each point $x \in M \setminus \Sigma$, the point $y = q^{-1}(s(x)) \in S$ has the property that $\pi \circ q(y) = x$. Let us take a point $x \in \Sigma$ and a sequence of points $\left\{ x_n \in M \setminus \Sigma \right\}$ converging to $x$. The sequence of points $y_n = q^{-1}(s(x_n)) \in S$ has a convergent subsequence $\left\{ y_{n_k} \right\}$ because $S$ is compact. If $y = \lim_{n_k \to \infty} y_{n_k}$, then \begin{equation} \pi \circ q(y) = \lim_{n_k \to \infty} \pi q(y_{n_k}) = \lim_{n_k \to \infty} x_{n_k} = x. \end{equation} c) As $\pi \circ q$ is surjective and $\pi \circ q(S \setminus \partial S) = M \setminus \Sigma$ because $q(S \setminus \partial S) = s(M \setminus \Sigma)$, we have that $\pi \circ q(\partial S) = \Sigma$. d) and e) For a point $x \in \Sigma$ let us take a neighborhood $U$ diffeomorphic to an open disk such that $U_0 = U \setminus \left\{ x \right\} \subset M \setminus \Sigma$. The closure $\overline{U_0} = \Gamma \sqcup U_0 \sqcup \left\{ x \right\}$, where $\Gamma$ is the boundary of $U$. Let $V_0 = q^{-1} s(U_0)$. Then $\pi \circ q(\overline{V_0}) = \overline{U_0}$ because $M$ and $S$ are compact. As $\pi \circ q : S \setminus \partial S \to M \setminus \Sigma$ is a diffeomorphism, and $\Gamma \subset M \setminus \Sigma$, we have a curve $C \subset (\overline{V_0} \setminus V_0) \cap (S \setminus \partial S)$ such that $\pi \circ q(C) = \Gamma$. This means that $C$ is a part of the boundary $\partial V_0$ which lies in the interior part of $S$. Now, by b) we know that $\pi^{-1}(x) \subset \sqcup_{i \in I} \partial S_i$, $I \subset \{1, \cdots, n\}$. Finally we have that $\overline{V_0} = C \sqcup V_0 \sqcup \left( \sqcup_{i \in I} \partial S_i \right)$, and we know that $V_0$ is diffeomorphic to $U_0$, and $C \subset S \setminus \partial S$ is diffeomorphic to $\Gamma$, that is $C$ is diffeomorphic to a circle $\mathbb{S}^1$. Thus $V_0$ is an open set in $S$ diffeomorphic to an open ring, and the boundary of $V_0$ consists of a closed curve in the interior part of $S$ and some components of the boundary of $S$. However, this means that the boundary of $V_0$ contains one and only one component $\partial S_i$ of $\partial S$, otherwise the fundamental group of $\pi_1(V_0) \not\cong \mathbb{Z}$. Thus we get the affirmation d) and the decomposition $V = \overline{V_0} = C \sqcup V_0 \sqcup \partial S_i$ with the properties given by~\eqref{eq:4}. Therefore, we have proved e).
nodes.statement_short: Item-by-item: invert $s$ for a); compactness of $S$ for surjectivity; then an annulus argument with $\pi_1(V_0)\cong\mathbb{Z}$ for d) and e).

nodes.name: Item a): inverse of the section
nodes.statement: a) $s : M \setminus \Sigma \to s(M \setminus \Sigma)$ is a diffeomorphism and $\left. \pi \right|_{s(M \setminus \Sigma)} : s(M \setminus \Sigma) \to M \setminus \Sigma$ is the diffeomorphism inverse to $s$. Therefore $\pi \circ q : S \setminus \partial S \to M \setminus \Sigma$ is a diffeomorphism
nodes.statement_short: Off the singular set $\pi$ inverts $s$, so $\pi\circ q$ is a diffeomorphism.
nodes.section: 2 Singularity of section and its index

nodes.name: Item b): surjectivity by compactness
nodes.statement: b) For each point $x \in M \setminus \Sigma$, the point $y = q^{-1}(s(x)) \in S$ has the property that $\pi \circ q(y) = x$. Let us take a point $x \in \Sigma$ and a sequence of points $\left\{ x_n \in M \setminus \Sigma \right\}$ converging to $x$. The sequence of points $y_n = q^{-1}(s(x_n)) \in S$ has a convergent subsequence $\left\{ y_{n_k} \right\}$ because $S$ is compact. If $y = \lim_{n_k \to \infty} y_{n_k}$, then \begin{equation} \pi \circ q(y) = \lim_{n_k \to \infty} \pi q(y_{n_k}) = \lim_{n_k \to \infty} x_{n_k} = x. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Take a sequence converging to a singular point and extract a convergent subsequence in the compact $S$.
nodes.section: 2 Singularity of section and its index

nodes.name: Item c): image of the boundary
nodes.statement: c) As $\pi \circ q$ is surjective and $\pi \circ q(S \setminus \partial S) = M \setminus \Sigma$ because $q(S \setminus \partial S) = s(M \setminus \Sigma)$, we have that $\pi \circ q(\partial S) = \Sigma$.
nodes.statement_short: Surjectivity plus $\pi\circ q(S\setminus\partial S)=M\setminus\Sigma$ forces $\pi\circ q(\partial S)=\Sigma$.
nodes.section: 2 Singularity of section and its index

nodes.name: Items d) and e): annular neighbourhood of a boundary component
nodes.statement: d) and e) For a point $x \in \Sigma$ let us take a neighborhood $U$ diffeomorphic to an open disk such that $U_0 = U \setminus \left\{ x \right\} \subset M \setminus \Sigma$. The closure $\overline{U_0} = \Gamma \sqcup U_0 \sqcup \left\{ x \right\}$, where $\Gamma$ is the boundary of $U$. Let $V_0 = q^{-1} s(U_0)$. Then $\pi \circ q(\overline{V_0}) = \overline{U_0}$ because $M$ and $S$ are compact. As $\pi \circ q : S \setminus \partial S \to M \setminus \Sigma$ is a diffeomorphism, and $\Gamma \subset M \setminus \Sigma$, we have a curve $C \subset (\overline{V_0} \setminus V_0) \cap (S \setminus \partial S)$ such that $\pi \circ q(C) = \Gamma$. This means that $C$ is a part of the boundary $\partial V_0$ which lies in the interior part of $S$. Now, by b) we know that $\pi^{-1}(x) \subset \sqcup_{i \in I} \partial S_i$, $I \subset \{1, \cdots, n\}$. Finally we have that $\overline{V_0} = C \sqcup V_0 \sqcup \left( \sqcup_{i \in I} \partial S_i \right)$, and we know that $V_0$ is diffeomorphic to $U_0$, and $C \subset S \setminus \partial S$ is diffeomorphic to $\Gamma$, that is $C$ is diffeomorphic to a circle $\mathbb{S}^1$. Thus $V_0$ is an open set in $S$ diffeomorphic to an open ring, and the boundary of $V_0$ consists of a closed curve in the interior part of $S$ and some components of the boundary of $S$. However, this means that the boundary of $V_0$ contains one and only one component $\partial S_i$ of $\partial S$, otherwise the fundamental group of $\pi_1(V_0) \not\cong \mathbb{Z}$. Thus we get the affirmation d) and the decomposition $V = \overline{V_0} = C \sqcup V_0 \sqcup \partial S_i$ with the properties given by~\eqref{eq:4}. Therefore, we have proved e).
nodes.statement_short: Pull back a punctured disc, identify its closure as an annulus, and use $\pi_1\cong\mathbb{Z}$ to see exactly one boundary component.

nodes.name: Collar neighbourhood $u_i$ of each boundary component
nodes.statement: From the proof of items d) and e) of Theorem~\ref{thm:1} it follows that, for each boundary component $\partial S_i$, we have a closed neighborhood $V_i$ of $\partial S_i$ and a diffeomorphism of manifolds with boundary $u_i : \mathbb{S}^1 \times [0, 1] \to V_i$ such that $u_i(\mathbb{S}^1 \times \left\{ 1 \right\} = \partial S_i$, $U = \pi \circ q \circ u_i(\mathbb{S}^1 \times [0, 1])$ is a closed neighborhood of $x_i \in \Sigma$ diffeomorphic to a disk, $\pi \circ q \circ u_i(\mathbb{S}^1 \times \left\{ 0 \right\}$ is the boundary of $U$, and $\pi \circ q \circ u_i(\mathbb{S}^1 \times \left\{ 1 \right\} = x$ (see Figure~\ref{fig:1}).
nodes.statement_short: Each boundary component has a collar $u_i:\mathbb{S}^1\times[0,1]\to V_i$ projecting onto a disc neighbourhood of the singular point.

nodes.name: Section of the unit circle bundle over $\mathbb{R}^2$ with winding $n$
nodes.statement: Let $\xi$ be a unit vector bundle of $\mathbb{R}^2$, $\pi : \mathbb{R}^2 \times \mathbb{S}^1 \to \mathbb{R}^2$, and consider a section $s : \mathbb{R}^2 \to E$ which takes value $s(\rho, \varphi) = (\cos n\varphi, \sin n\varphi)$ with respect to the polar coordinate system on $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus (0, 0)$. The point $(0, 0)$ is the singular point of this section. If we take the coordinate system $(\rho, \varphi, \psi)$ on $\pi^{-1}(\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus (0, 0))$, then $s(\rho, \varphi) = (\rho, \varphi, n\varphi)$. Now the map $u : \mathbb{S}^1 \times [0, 1] \to E$ is given with respect to coordinates $(x, y, \psi)$ on $E = \mathbb{R}^2 \times \mathbb{S}^1$ by $u(\alpha, t) = ( (1 - t)\cos\alpha, (1-t)\sin\alpha, n \alpha)$. Therefore $u( \mathbb{S}^1 \times \left\{ 0 \right\})$ is a curve consisting of helices, $u( \mathbb{S}^1 \times \left\{ 1 \right\})$ is the fiber $(0, 0) \times \mathbb{S}^1 \subset E$ represents the image of $u$.
nodes.statement_short: The section $(\cos n\varphi,\sin n\varphi)$ of $\mathbb{R}^2\times\mathbb{S}^1$ has a singularity at the origin resolved by a helical cylinder.

nodes.name: Chart-independent isomorphisms $\pi_*(\eta_x)$, $H_*(\eta_x)$, $H^*(\eta_x)$
nodes.statement: This means that for any $x \in M$ we have well defined isomorphisms of the homotopy and (co)homology groups: \begin{equation} \begin{array}{l} \pi_*(\eta_x) : \pi_*(F_x) \to \pi_*(F), \\[5pt] H_*(\eta_x) : H_*(F_x) \to H_*(F), \quad H^*(\eta_x) : H^*(F) \to H^*(F_x), \end{array} \end{equation} which do not depend on the chart.
nodes.statement_short: Connectedness of $G$ makes the fibrewise identifications of homotopy and (co)homology groups independent of the chart.

nodes.name: index of the section $s$ at the point $x_i \in \Sigma$
nodes.statement: For $x_i \in \Sigma$ the map $q \circ u_i : \mathbb{S}^1 \times [0, 1] \to E$ restricted to $\mathbb{S}^1 \times \left\{ 1 \right\}$ gives a map $\gamma_i : \mathbb{S}^1 \to F_{x_i}$, and therefore an element $ind_{x_i}(s) \in \pi_1(F)$ via the isomorphism $\pi_1(\eta_x)$ (see~\eqref{eq:8}). This element $ind_{x_i}(s)$ will be called the \emph{index of the section $s$ at the point $x_i \in \Sigma$}.
nodes.statement_short: The index of $s$ at a singular point is the class in $\pi_1(F)$ of the loop traced by the resolution on the boundary circle.

nodes.name: Index of the winding-$n$ section
nodes.statement: The index of the section $s$ at the point $(0, 0)$ in Example~\ref{ex:1} is equal to $n \gamma$, where $\gamma$ is a generator of the group $\pi_1(\mathbb{S}^1)$.

nodes.name: index $ind_{x_i}(s;a)$ with respect to a class $a \in H^1(F)$
nodes.statement: For $a \in H^1(F)$ we define the \emph{index $ind_{x_i}(s;a)$ of the section $s$ at the point $x_i \in \Sigma$ with respect to $a$} as \begin{equation} ind_{x_i}(s;a) = \langle a, ind_{x_i}(s) \rangle = \int_\gamma \alpha = \int_{\mathbb{S}^1} \gamma^* \alpha, \end{equation} where $\gamma : \mathbb{S}^1 \to F$ is the curve representing the element $ind_{x_i}(s) \in \pi_1(F)$ and $\alpha \in \Omega^1(F)$ is a closed form representing the element $a \in H^1(F)$. \emph{The index of a section $s$ with respect to $a$} is the number \begin{equation} ind(s; a) = \sum_{x_i \in \Sigma} ind_{x_i}(s;a). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Pairing the homotopy index with a $1$-cohomology class $a$ gives a number; summing over $\Sigma$ gives $ind(s;a)$.

nodes.name: Integral form of $ind_{x_i}(s;a)$
nodes.statement: By~\eqref{eq:11}, \begin{equation} ind_{x_i}(s;a) = \int_{\gamma_i} \eta_x^*\alpha, \end{equation} where $[\alpha] = a$ and $\gamma_i$ is defined in Definition~\ref{df:1}.

nodes.name: Index with respect to the angular form
nodes.statement: Let $a = [ d\phi ] \in H^1(\mathbb{S}^1; \mathbb{R})$, where $d\phi$ is the angular form on $\mathbb{S}^1$, then $a$ is a base of $H^1(\mathbb{S}^1; \mathbb{R})$. Then index of the section $s$ at the point $(0, 0)$ in Example~\ref{ex:1} with respect to $a$ is equal to $n$.

nodes.name: vertical distribution
nodes.statement: Let us denote by $V$ the \emph{vertical distribution}, that is the distribution of the tangent spaces to the fibers, then we have $TE = H \oplus V$.

nodes.name: Existence of a vertical $1$-form representing $a \in H^1(F)$
nodes.statement: Let $a \in H^1(F)$ and $H$ be a connection in $E$. There exists a $1$-form $\alpha \in \Omega^1(E)$ such that \begin{enumerate} \item $\left.\alpha\right|_H = 0$; \item for each $x \in M$, $d i_x^* \alpha = 0$ and $[ i_x^* \alpha ] = H^1(\eta_x) a$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Given a connection $H$ and a class $a\in H^1(F)$ there is a $1$-form on $E$ vanishing on $H$ whose fibre restriction is closed and represents $a$.
assumptions: Let $a \in H^1(F)$ and $H$ be a connection in $E$.
conclusions: There exists a $1$-form $\alpha \in \Omega^1(E)$ such that
$\left.\alpha\right|_H = 0$;
for each $x \in M$, $d i_x^* \alpha = 0$ and $[ i_x^* \alpha ] = H^1(\eta_x) a$.

nodes.name: Proof of the existence of the vertical form $\alpha$
nodes.statement: Let us take an atlas $(U_i, \psi_i)$ of the bundle $\xi$, and fix a $1$-form $\bar\alpha \in \Omega^1(F)$ such that $[\bar\alpha] = a$. Let $\rho_i$ be the partition of unity subordinate to the covering $\left\{ U_i \right\}$, and $\eta_i : \pi^{-1}(U_i) \to F$ (see~\eqref{eq:6}). Then take the collection of $1$-forms $\bar\alpha_i = \eta^*_i \bar\alpha \in \Omega^1(\pi^{-1}(U_i))$, and then construct $\widetilde{\alpha} = \sum_i \pi^*\rho_i\, \bar\alpha_i \in \Omega^1(V)$. Then \begin{equation} i_x^* \widetilde{\alpha} = \sum_i \rho_i(x)\, i_x^* \bar\alpha_i = \sum_i \rho_i(x)\, i_x^* \eta_i^* \bar\alpha \in \Omega^1(F_x). \end{equation} Therefore, \begin{equation} d i_x^* \widetilde{\alpha} = \sum_i \rho_i(x)\, i_x^* \eta_i^* d\bar\alpha = 0 \end{equation} and \begin{equation} [ i_x^* \widetilde{\alpha} ] = \sum_i \rho_i(x)\, [ i_x^* \eta_i^* \bar\alpha ] = a, \end{equation} because $\sum_i \rho_i(x) = 1$. We have the decomposition $TE = H \oplus V$, and therefore we can define the desired $\alpha \in \Omega^1(E)$ by $\left.\alpha\right|_H = 0$ and $\left.\alpha\right|_{V} = \widetilde{\alpha}$.
nodes.statement_short: Glue local pullbacks $\eta_i^*\bar\alpha$ with a partition of unity, then extend by zero along $H$.

nodes.name: Glue local forms with a partition of unity
nodes.statement: Let us take an atlas $(U_i, \psi_i)$ of the bundle $\xi$, and fix a $1$-form $\bar\alpha \in \Omega^1(F)$ such that $[\bar\alpha] = a$. Let $\rho_i$ be the partition of unity subordinate to the covering $\left\{ U_i \right\}$, and $\eta_i : \pi^{-1}(U_i) \to F$ (see~\eqref{eq:6}). Then take the collection of $1$-forms $\bar\alpha_i = \eta^*_i \bar\alpha \in \Omega^1(\pi^{-1}(U_i))$, and then construct $\widetilde{\alpha} = \sum_i \pi^*\rho_i\, \bar\alpha_i \in \Omega^1(V)$.
nodes.statement_short: Build $\widetilde\alpha$ from local pullbacks of $\bar\alpha$ via a subordinate partition of unity.

nodes.name: Check closedness and cohomology class on fibres
nodes.statement: Then \begin{equation} i_x^* \widetilde{\alpha} = \sum_i \rho_i(x)\, i_x^* \bar\alpha_i = \sum_i \rho_i(x)\, i_x^* \eta_i^* \bar\alpha \in \Omega^1(F_x). \end{equation} Therefore, \begin{equation} d i_x^* \widetilde{\alpha} = \sum_i \rho_i(x)\, i_x^* \eta_i^* d\bar\alpha = 0 \end{equation} and \begin{equation} [ i_x^* \widetilde{\alpha} ] = \sum_i \rho_i(x)\, [ i_x^* \eta_i^* \bar\alpha ] = a, \end{equation} because $\sum_i \rho_i(x) = 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Restricting to a fibre gives a closed form whose class is $a$ since the $\rho_i$ sum to $1$.

nodes.name: Extend by zero along the horizontal distribution
nodes.statement: We have the decomposition $TE = H \oplus V$, and therefore we can define the desired $\alpha \in \Omega^1(E)$ by $\left.\alpha\right|_H = 0$ and $\left.\alpha\right|_{V} = \widetilde{\alpha}$.
nodes.statement_short: Use $TE=H\oplus V$ to define $\alpha$ with $\alpha|_H=0$ and $\alpha|_V=\widetilde\alpha$.

nodes.statement_short: A covariant derivative defined only along a distribution $\Delta$, satisfying the usual linearity and Leibniz rules.

nodes.name: Extension of $d$ to a bundle-valued differential $D$
nodes.statement: Let $\xi = (\pi : E \to B)$ be a vector bundle of rank $r$ over a manifold $B$, and $\nabla$ be a linear connection in this bundle. Then we can extend the exterior differential $d : \Omega^q(B) \to \Omega^{q + 1}(B)$ to a differential operator $D : \Omega^q(B) \otimes \Gamma(\xi) \to \Omega^{q + 1}(B) \otimes \Gamma(\xi)$, where $\Gamma(\xi)$ is the module of sections of $\xi$ so that \begin{equation} D(\omega \otimes s) = d\omega \otimes s + (-1)^{|\omega|} \omega \wedge \nabla s. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: A linear connection extends the exterior differential to bundle-valued forms via the Leibniz rule.
assumptions: Let $\xi = (\pi : E \to B)$ be a vector bundle of rank $r$ over a manifold $B$, and $\nabla$ be a linear connection in this bundle.
conclusions: Then we can extend the exterior differential $d : \Omega^q(B) \to \Omega^{q + 1}(B)$ to a differential operator $D : \Omega^q(B) \otimes \Gamma(\xi) \to \Omega^{q + 1}(B) \otimes \Gamma(\xi)$, where $\Gamma(\xi)$ is the module of sections of $\xi$ so that
D(\omega \otimes s) = d\omega \otimes s + (-1)^{|\omega|} \omega \wedge \nabla s.

nodes.name: Proof that $D$ is well defined
nodes.statement:
Let $\{e_\alpha\}_{\alpha = \overline{1, r}}$ be a local frame field of $\xi$ over $U \subset B$. Then any $\omega \in \Omega^q(B) \otimes \Gamma(\xi)$ restricted to $U$ can be written in the form $\omega = \omega^\alpha e_\alpha$. If we change the frame field to $\{e_{\alpha'}\}_{\alpha' = \overline{1, r}}$, then $e_{\alpha'} = A_{\alpha'}^\alpha e_\alpha$ and $\omega^{\alpha'} = A_{\alpha}^{\alpha'}\omega^\alpha$, where $A_{\alpha'}^\alpha$ are functions on $U$. Then,  egin{multline} D(\omega^{\alpha'} e_{\alpha'}) = d\omega^{\alpha'} e_{\alpha'}+ (-1)^q \omega^{\alpha'} \wedge 
abla e_{\alpha'} = d( A_ eta^{\alpha'} \omega^ eta ) A_{\alpha'}^\alpha e_\alpha + (-1)^q \omega^{\alpha'} \wedge 
abla (A_{\alpha'}^\alpha e_\alpha) \ = d A_ eta^{\alpha'} \wedge \omega^ eta A_{\alpha'}^\alpha e_\alpha+ A_ eta^{\alpha'} d\omega^ eta A_{\alpha'}^\alpha e_\alpha+ (-1)^q \omega^{\alpha'} \wedge dA_{\alpha'}^\alpha e_\alpha+ (-1)^q \omega^{\alpha'} \wedge A_{\alpha'}^\alpha 
abla e_\alpha \ = (A_{\alpha'}^\alpha d A_ eta^{\alpha'} \wedge \omega^ eta + (-1)^q \omega^{ eta} \wedge A_ eta^{\alpha'} dA_{\alpha'}^\alpha) e_\alpha+ d\omega^\alpha e_\alpha+ (-1)^q \omega^{\alpha} \wedge 
abla e_\alpha \ = (A_{\alpha'}^\alpha d A_ eta^{\alpha'} + A_ eta^{\alpha'} dA_{\alpha'}^\alpha) \wedge \omega^{ eta} e_\alpha + D(\omega^\alpha e_\alpha) = D(\omega^\alpha e_\alpha), \end{multline} because $A_{\alpha'}^\alpha d A_ eta^{\alpha'} + A_ eta^{\alpha'} dA_{\alpha'}^\alpha = d( A_{\alpha'}^\alpha A_ eta^{\alpha'} ) = d \, \delta_ eta^\alpha = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Frame-independence: the transition terms cancel because $A_{\alpha'}^\alpha dA_\beta^{\alpha'}+A_\beta^{\alpha'}dA_{\alpha'}^\alpha=d\delta^\alpha_\beta=0$.

nodes.name: Fix a local frame field
nodes.statement: Let $\{e_\alpha\}_{\alpha = \overline{1, r}}$ be a local frame field of $\xi$ over $U \subset B$. Then any $\omega \in \Omega^q(B) \otimes \Gamma(\xi)$ restricted to $U$ can be written in the form $\omega = \omega^\alpha e_\alpha$.
nodes.statement_short: Write a bundle-valued form in a local frame.

nodes.name: Change the frame field
nodes.statement: If we change the frame field to $\{e_{\alpha'}\}_{\alpha' = \overline{1, r}}$, then $e_{\alpha'} = A_{\alpha'}^\alpha e_\alpha$ and $\omega^{\alpha'} = A_{\alpha}^{\alpha'}\omega^\alpha$, where $A_{\alpha'}^\alpha$ are functions on $U$.
nodes.statement_short: Record how components and frame transform under $A$.

nodes.name: Expand and cancel the transition terms
nodes.statement:
Then,  egin{multline} D(\omega^{\alpha'} e_{\alpha'}) = d\omega^{\alpha'} e_{\alpha'}+ (-1)^q \omega^{\alpha'} \wedge 
abla e_{\alpha'} = d( A_ eta^{\alpha'} \omega^ eta ) A_{\alpha'}^\alpha e_\alpha + (-1)^q \omega^{\alpha'} \wedge 
abla (A_{\alpha'}^\alpha e_\alpha) \ = d A_ eta^{\alpha'} \wedge \omega^ eta A_{\alpha'}^\alpha e_\alpha+ A_ eta^{\alpha'} d\omega^ eta A_{\alpha'}^\alpha e_\alpha+ (-1)^q \omega^{\alpha'} \wedge dA_{\alpha'}^\alpha e_\alpha+ (-1)^q \omega^{\alpha'} \wedge A_{\alpha'}^\alpha 
abla e_\alpha \ = (A_{\alpha'}^\alpha d A_ eta^{\alpha'} \wedge \omega^ eta + (-1)^q \omega^{ eta} \wedge A_ eta^{\alpha'} dA_{\alpha'}^\alpha) e_\alpha+ d\omega^\alpha e_\alpha+ (-1)^q \omega^{\alpha} \wedge 
abla e_\alpha \ = (A_{\alpha'}^\alpha d A_ eta^{\alpha'} + A_ eta^{\alpha'} dA_{\alpha'}^\alpha) \wedge \omega^{ eta} e_\alpha + D(\omega^\alpha e_\alpha) = D(\omega^\alpha e_\alpha), \end{multline} because $A_{\alpha'}^\alpha d A_ eta^{\alpha'} + A_ eta^{\alpha'} dA_{\alpha'}^\alpha = d( A_{\alpha'}^\alpha A_ eta^{\alpha'} ) = d \, \delta_ eta^\alpha = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Expanding $D$ in the new frame, the derivative-of-transition terms cancel, so $D$ is frame independent.

nodes.name: $D^2$ and the curvature tensor
nodes.statement: $D^2 (\omega \otimes s) = \omega \wedge R(s)$, where $R$ is the curvature tensor of the linear connection $\nabla$.

nodes.name: Formula for $D\omega$ on vector fields
nodes.statement: For $\omega \in \Omega^1(B) \otimes \Gamma(E)$, and $X, Y \in \mathfrak{X}(B)$, \begin{equation} D\omega(X, Y) = \nabla_X (\omega(Y)) - \nabla_Y (\omega(X)) - \omega([X, Y]). \end{equation}
assumptions: For $\omega \in \Omega^1(B) \otimes \Gamma(E)$, and $X, Y \in \mathfrak{X}(B)$,
conclusions: D\omega(X, Y) = \nabla_X (\omega(Y)) - \nabla_Y (\omega(X)) - \omega([X, Y]).

nodes.name: Proof of the formula for $D\omega$
nodes.statement_short: Expand both sides in a local frame; the terms reassemble into $d\omega^\alpha e_\alpha-\omega^\alpha\wedge\nabla e_\alpha$.

nodes.name: Differentiate in a local frame
nodes.statement_short: Compute $\nabla_X(\omega(Y))$ componentwise in the frame $\{e_\alpha\}$.

nodes.name: Assemble the three terms into $D\omega$
nodes.statement_short: Combining the three terms gives exactly $D\omega(X,Y)$.

nodes.name: Structure equations
nodes.statement: Let $\omega : TE \to V$ be the connection form of the connection $H$. Then \begin{equation} D\omega = \Omega, \end{equation} where $\Omega(X, Y) = D\omega(X^h, Y^h) \in \Omega^2(E) \otimes \mathfrak{X}^V(E)$ is horizontal.
nodes.statement_short: The covariant differential of the connection form is the horizontal curvature form: $D\omega=\Omega$.
assumptions: Let $\omega : TE \to V$ be the connection form of the connection $H$.
conclusions: D\omega = \Omega,
where $\Omega(X, Y) = D\omega(X^h, Y^h) \in \Omega^2(E) \otimes \mathfrak{X}^V(E)$ is horizontal.

nodes.name: Proof of the structure equations
nodes.statement:
It is sufficient to prove that $D\omega(X, Y) = 0$ if $Y \in \mathfrak{X}^v(E)$. We will apply~\eqref{eq:22}. If $X \in \mathfrak{X}^h(E)$, then  egin{equation} D\omega(X, Y) = 
abla_X \omega(Y) - 
abla_Y \omega(X) - \omega( [X, Y] ) = 
abla_X Y - \omega( [X, Y] ) = 0 \end{equation} by the definition of $
abla$ (see~\eqref{eq:18} and~\eqref{eq:19}). If $X \in \mathfrak{X}^v(E)$, then  egin{equation} D\omega(X, Y) = 
abla_X \omega(Y) - 
abla_Y \omega(X) - \omega( [X, Y] ) = 0 \end{equation} again by the definition of $
abla$ and because the connection $
abla^V$ is torsion free.
nodes.statement_short: Show $D\omega$ kills vertical arguments, splitting into the horizontal and vertical cases via the definition of $\nabla$ and torsion-freeness of $\nabla^V$.

nodes.name: Reduce to vanishing on vertical arguments
nodes.statement: It is sufficient to prove that $D\omega(X, Y) = 0$ if $Y \in \mathfrak{X}^v(E)$. We will apply~\eqref{eq:22}.
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to show $D\omega(X,Y)=0$ whenever $Y$ is vertical; apply the formula for $D\omega$.

nodes.name: Case $X$ horizontal
nodes.statement:
If $X \in \mathfrak{X}^h(E)$, then  egin{equation} D\omega(X, Y) = 
abla_X \omega(Y) - 
abla_Y \omega(X) - \omega( [X, Y] ) = 
abla_X Y - \omega( [X, Y] ) = 0 \end{equation} by the definition of $
abla$ (see~\eqref{eq:18} and~\eqref{eq:19}).
nodes.statement_short: For horizontal $X$ the terms cancel by the definition of $\nabla^H$.

nodes.name: Case $X$ vertical
nodes.statement:
If $X \in \mathfrak{X}^v(E)$, then  egin{equation} D\omega(X, Y) = 
abla_X \omega(Y) - 
abla_Y \omega(X) - \omega( [X, Y] ) = 0 \end{equation} again by the definition of $
abla$ and because the connection $
abla^V$ is torsion free.
nodes.statement_short: For vertical $X$ the expression vanishes because $\nabla^V$ is torsion free.

nodes.name: curvature form of the connection $H$
nodes.statement: The tensor $\Omega \in \Omega^2(E) \otimes \mathfrak{X}^V(E)$ is called the \emph{curvature form of the connection $H$}.

nodes.name: Vanishing curvature characterizes integrability of $H$
nodes.statement: The curvature form $\Omega$ vanishes if and only if $H$ is integrable.
assumptions: Let $H$ be a connection in the fiber bundle $E$.
conclusions: The curvature form $\Omega$ vanishes if and only if $H$ is integrable.

nodes.name: Proof that $\Omega=0$ iff $H$ is integrable
nodes.statement: Indeed, by Statement~\ref{stat:3}, we have that, for any horizontal vector fields $X$ and $Y$, \begin{equation} D\omega(X, Y) = - \omega([X, Y]), \end{equation} therefore $D\omega(X^h, Y^h) = 0$, for any $X^h$ and $Y^h$ if and only if the Lie bracket of horizontal vector fields is again a horizontal vector field, this is equivalent to integrability of $H$.
nodes.statement_short: $D\omega(X,Y)=-\omega([X,Y])$ on horizontal fields, so $\Omega=0$ exactly when horizontal fields are closed under the bracket.

nodes.name: Bidegree decomposition of $d\alpha$
nodes.statement: The form $\alpha$ constructed in Statement~\ref{stat:1} lies in $\Omega^{(0, 1)}(E)$ and $d \alpha = \theta_{(1, 1)} + \theta_{(2, 0)}$, where $\theta_{(1, 1)} \in \Omega^{(1, 1)}$ and $\theta_{(2, 0)} \in \Omega^{(2, 0)}$, and \begin{equation} \theta_{(1, 1)}(X, Y) = (L_X \alpha)(Y), \quad \theta_{(2, 0)} = \widetilde{\alpha}(\Omega). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $d\alpha$ splits into a $(1,1)$-part given by the Lie derivative of $\alpha$ and a $(2,0)$-part $\widetilde\alpha(\Omega)$.
assumptions: The form $\alpha$ constructed in Statement~\ref{stat:1} lies in $\Omega^{(0, 1)}(E)$
conclusions: $d \alpha = \theta_{(1, 1)} + \theta_{(2, 0)}$, where $\theta_{(1, 1)} \in \Omega^{(1, 1)}$ and $\theta_{(2, 0)} \in \Omega^{(2, 0)}$
\theta_{(1, 1)}(X, Y) = (L_X \alpha)(Y), \quad \theta_{(2, 0)} = \widetilde{\alpha}(\Omega).

nodes.name: Generalized Gauss-Bonnet formula for sections with singularities
nodes.statement: For $a \in H^1(F)$, let $\alpha \in \Omega^1(E)$ be the corresponding vertical form constructed in Statement~\ref{stat:1}. Also let $d\alpha = \theta_{(1, 1)} + \theta_{(2, 0)}$ as in Statement~\ref{stat:5}. Then \begin{equation} \int\limits_S q^*\theta_{(1, 1)} + q^*\alpha(\Omega) = \sum\limits_{i = \overline{1, k}} index_{x_i}(s; a). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The sum of the indices of a singular section equals the integral over the resolving surface $S$ of the $2$-form built from the connection.
assumptions: For $a \in H^1(F)$, let $\alpha \in \Omega^1(E)$ be the corresponding vertical form constructed in Statement~\ref{stat:1}.
Also let $d\alpha = \theta_{(1, 1)} + \theta_{(2, 0)}$ as in Statement~\ref{stat:5}.
conclusions: \int\limits_S q^*\theta_{(1, 1)} + q^*\alpha(\Omega) = \sum\limits_{i = \overline{1, k}} index_{x_i}(s; a).

nodes.name: Proof of the generalized Gauss-Bonnet formula
nodes.statement: By the Stokes theorem, \begin{equation} \int_S d q^* \alpha = \int_{\partial S} q^*\alpha = \sum\limits_{i=1}^k \int_{\partial S_i} q^*\alpha. \end{equation} We have that \begin{equation} \int_{\partial S_i} q^*\alpha = \int_{\mathbb{S}^1 \times \{ 1 \}} u_i^* q^* \alpha = \int_{\mathbb{S}^1} \gamma_i^* \alpha = \int_{\gamma_i} \alpha = ind_{x_i}(s; a), \end{equation} Therefore, \begin{equation} \sum\limits_{i=1}^k \int_{\partial S_i} q^*\alpha = ind_{x_i}(s; a). \end{equation} On the other hand, by Statement~\ref{stat:5}, \begin{equation} \int_S d q^* \alpha = \int_S q^* d\alpha = \int_S q^*\theta_{(1, 1)} + q^*\theta_{(2, 0)}. \end{equation} and thus we get the required statement.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Stokes' theorem to $q^*\alpha$ on $S$: the boundary integrals are the indices, the interior integral is the curvature term.

nodes.name: Apply Stokes' theorem on $S$
nodes.statement: By the Stokes theorem, \begin{equation} \int_S d q^* \alpha = \int_{\partial S} q^*\alpha = \sum\limits_{i=1}^k \int_{\partial S_i} q^*\alpha. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Stokes converts $\int_S dq^*\alpha$ into a sum of boundary integrals.

nodes.name: Identify each boundary integral with an index
nodes.statement: We have that \begin{equation} \int_{\partial S_i} q^*\alpha = \int_{\mathbb{S}^1 \times \{ 1 \}} u_i^* q^* \alpha = \int_{\mathbb{S}^1} \gamma_i^* \alpha = \int_{\gamma_i} \alpha = ind_{x_i}(s; a), \end{equation} Therefore, \begin{equation} \sum\limits_{i=1}^k \int_{\partial S_i} q^*\alpha = ind_{x_i}(s; a). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Pulling back by the collar $u_i$ identifies $\int_{\partial S_i}q^*\alpha$ with $ind_{x_i}(s;a)$.

nodes.name: Evaluate the left-hand side by the bidegree splitting
nodes.statement: On the other hand, by Statement~\ref{stat:5}, \begin{equation} \int_S d q^* \alpha = \int_S q^* d\alpha = \int_S q^*\theta_{(1, 1)} + q^*\theta_{(2, 0)}. \end{equation} and thus we get the required statement.
nodes.statement_short: Replace $d\alpha$ by $\theta_{(1,1)}+\theta_{(2,0)}$ to obtain the claimed identity.

nodes.name: Geometric meaning of the prolongation assumption
nodes.statement: In geometric terms, our assumption means that the angle $\psi$ of the unit vector field $s$ with the vector field $e_1$ (see~\eqref{eq:39}) has limit when we approach to the point $x_i$ by some curve, but the limit depends on the curve.

nodes.name: Local expression $\alpha = \theta + \pi^* G$ of the vertical form
nodes.statement: In terms of the trivialization \begin{equation} U \times \mathbb{S}^1 \to \pi^{-1}(U), \quad (q, \psi) \mapsto \cos\psi e_1(q) + \sin\psi e_2(q). \end{equation} where $U \subset M$ and $\left\{ e_1, e_2 \right\}$ is an orthonormal frame field, the form $\alpha$ is written as follows: \begin{equation} \alpha = \theta + \pi^* G, \end{equation} where $\nabla e_1 = G e_2$ and $\nabla e_2 = -G e_1$, and $G = G^2_{11} e^1 + G^2_{12} e^2$, $G^k_{ij}$ are the connection coefficients of $G$ with respect to the orthonormal frame $\left\{ e_1, e_2 \right\}$.
nodes.statement_short: In an orthonormal-frame trivialization the vertical form is the angular form plus the pullback of the Levi-Civita connection form.

nodes.name: $\alpha$ is the Levi-Civita connection form in the trivialization
nodes.statement: If $W = \cos\psi e_1 + \sin\psi e_2$, then $\nabla W = (d\psi + G)(-\sin\psi e_1 + \cos\psi e_2) = (d\psi + G) W^\perp$, therefore $W(t) = (\gamma(t), \psi(t))$ is parallel if and only if $\frac{d}{dt}\psi + G(\frac{d}{dt}\gamma) = 0$. This means that, in terms of the trivialization, the connection form is exactly the form $\alpha$ given by~\eqref{eq:42}. Therefore $\alpha$ vanishes over $H$ (condition (1) in Statement~\ref{stat:1}). At the same $\alpha$ restricted to a fiber is $\theta$, this means satisfies condition (2) in Statement~\ref{stat:1}.

nodes.name: Classical Hopf-Poincaré-Gauss-Bonnet theorem recovered
nodes.statement: we get the classical result \begin{equation} \int_M K e^1 \wedge e^2 = \sum_{i = \overline{1, k}} Ind_{x_i}(s). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Total Gaussian curvature equals the sum of the indices of the vector field.
assumptions: At the same time, by the construction, $\pi \circ q : S \setminus \partial S \to M \setminus \Sigma$ is a diffeomorphism, $\Sigma$ is a set of measure zero, and $K e^1 \wedge e^2$ is a $2$-form defined globally on $M$
conclusions: \int_M K e^1 \wedge e^2 = \sum_{i = \overline{1, k}} Ind_{x_i}(s).

nodes.name: projective bundle
nodes.statement: A \emph{projective bundle} is a locally trivial bundle $Q \to M$ with typical fiber $\mathbb{R}P^n$ and structure group $PGL(n)$. The number $n$ is called the \emph{rank} of $Q$.
differentia: with typical fiber $\mathbb{R}P^n$ and structure group $PGL(n)$

nodes.name: Projectivization $P(E)$ of a vector bundle
nodes.statement: Let $E \to M$ be a vector bundle. Then the bundle $P(E)$ of $1$-dimensional subspaces of the fibers of $E$ is called the \emph{projectivization} of $E$ and it is projective bundle.

nodes.name: orientable projective bundle
nodes.statement: If the structure group $PGL(n)$ of a projective bundle $Q$ reduces to $PGL_{+}(n)$, then $Q$ is called \emph{orientable}, on the contrary $Q$ is called \emph{no orientable}.

nodes.name: Projectivization of a non-orientable vector bundle
nodes.statement: If a vector bundle $E$ is no orientable, then $P(E)$ is no orientable.

nodes.name: Čech obstruction to lifting a $G$-bundle to $\widetilde{G}$
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item The \v Cech cochain $z$ is a normalized cocycle. \item The \v Cech cohomology class $[ z ] \in \check{H}^2(M; Z)$ is trivial if and only if there exists a $\widetilde{G}$-principal bundle $\widetilde{P}$ such that $P \cong \widetilde{P}/Z$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: The cochain built from lifted transition functions is a normalized $Z$-valued cocycle whose class vanishes exactly when a $\widetilde G$-bundle with $P\cong\widetilde P/Z$ exists.
assumptions: Let $P \to M$ be a $G$-principal bundle, $\mathcal{U} = \left\{ U_i \right\}$ be a good covering of a manifold $M$, and $g_{ij} : U_{ij} \to M$ be the transition functions of $M$.
Consider the Cech cochain $z = \left\{ z_{ijk} : U_{ijk} \to \widetilde{G} \right\}$ over the covering $\mathcal{U}$, where
conclusions: The \v Cech cochain $z$ is a normalized cocycle.
The \v Cech cohomology class $[ z ] \in \check{H}^2(M; Z)$ is trivial if and only if there exists a $\widetilde{G}$-principal bundle $\widetilde{P}$ such that $P \cong \widetilde{P}/Z$.

nodes.name: Proof of the Čech cocycle property and the lifting criterion
nodes.statement: Let us prove that $\left\{ z_{ijk} \right\}$ is a \v Chech cocycle on $\mathcal{U}$. First of all note that we have \begin{equation} \widetilde{g}_{ij} \widetilde{g}_{jk} = z_{ijk} \widetilde{g}_{ik} = \widetilde{g}_{ik} z_{ijk}. \end{equation} Then \begin{equation} (\widetilde{g}_{ij} \widetilde{g}_{jk}) \widetilde{g}_{ki} = z_{ijk} \widetilde{g}_{ik} \widetilde{g}_{ki} = z_{ijk} \text{ and } \widetilde{g}_{ij} (\widetilde{g}_{jk} \widetilde{g}_{ki}) = \widetilde{g}_{ij} \widetilde{g}_{ji} z_{jki} = z_{jki}, \end{equation} therefore $z_{ijk} = z_{kij} = z_{jki}$. At the same time, \begin{equation} z_{ijk}^{-1} \widetilde{g}_{ik}^{-1} = \left( z_{ijk} \widetilde{g}_{ik} \right)^{-1} = \left( \widetilde{g}_{ij} \widetilde{g}_{jk} \right)^{-1} = \widetilde{g}_{kj} \widetilde{g}_{ji} = z_{kji} \widetilde{g}_{ki}, \end{equation} hence follows that $z_{ijk}^{-1} = z_{kji} = z_{jik}$. Moreover $z_{ijk} = 1$ if at least two indices coincide. Thus $z = \left\{ z_{ijk} \right\}$ is a normalized cochain. Now we have \begin{equation} (\widetilde{g}_{ij} \widetilde{g}_{jk}) (\widetilde{g}_{kj} \widetilde{g}_{jl}) = z_{ijk} \widetilde{g}_{ik} z_{kjl} \widetilde{g}_{kl} = z_{ijk} z_{kjl} z_{ikl} g_{il} \end{equation} and \begin{equation} (\widetilde{g}_{ij} \widetilde{g}_{jk}) (\widetilde{g}_{kj} \widetilde{g}_{jl}) = (\widetilde{g}_{ij} (\widetilde{g}_{jk} (\widetilde{g}_{kj}) \widetilde{g}_{jl} = \widetilde{g}_{ij} \widetilde{g}_{jl} = z_{ijl} \widetilde{g}_{il}, \end{equation} thus $z_{ijk} z_{kjl} z_{ikl} = z_{ijl}$, this implies \begin{equation} \delta z = z_{jkl} z_{ikl}^{-1} z_{ijl} z_{ijk}^{-1} = 0. \end{equation} If $z = \delta u$, where $u = \left\{ u_{ij} \in Z \right\}$, then \begin{equation} z_{ijk} = u_{ij} u_{jk} u_{ki}. \end{equation} Therefore we can construct the $\widetilde{G}$-principal bundle $\widetilde{P} \to M$ with the transition functions $\widetilde{g}'_{ij} = \widetilde{g}_{ij} u_{ji}$ because \begin{equation} \widetilde{g}'_{ij} \widetilde{g}'_{jk} \widetilde{g}'_{ki} =\widetilde{g}_{ij} u_{ji} \widetilde{g}_{jk} u_{kj} \widetilde{g}_{ki} u_{ik} =\widetilde{g}_{ij} \widetilde{g}_{jk} \widetilde{g}_{ki} u_{ji} u_{kj} u_{ik} = z_{ijk} u_{ji} u_{kj} u_{ik} = 1. \end{equation} Now we have that $p(\widetilde{g}'_{ij}) = g_{ij}$ and from the following lemma it follows that there exists a principal bundle morphism $\pi : \widetilde{P} \to P$ written with respect to the trivializations as $(x, \widetilde{g}) \to (x, p(\widetilde{g}))$. \begin{lm} Let $G_a$, $a = 1, 2$ be Lie groups. Let $\pi_a : P_a \to M$, $a = 1, 2$ be a $G_a$-principal bundle and $f : G_1 \to G_2$ be a Lie group homomorphism. Assume that $\mathcal{U} = \left\{ U_i \right\}$ is a trivializing covering for $P_1$ and $P_2$ at the same time. If the transition functions $g^a_{ij}$ with respect to the covering $\mathcal{U}$ are related by $f(g^1_{ij}) = g^2_{ij}$, then there exists a principal fiber bundle homomorphism $F : P_1 \to P_2$ corresponding to $f$, i.\, e. $F(p_1 g_1) = F(p_1) f(g_1)$. \end{lm} \begin{proof} We define $F_i : \pi_1^{-1}(U_i) \to \pi_2^{-1}(U_i)$ by the commutative diagram \begin{equation} \xymatrix{ \pi_1^{-1}(U_i) \ar[r]^{F_i} \ar[d]_{\psi_i^1} & \pi_2^{-1}(U_i) \ar[d]^{\psi_i^2} \\ U_i \times G_1 \ar[r]^{ 1 \times f} & U_i \times G_2 } \end{equation} where $\psi_a$ are the trivializations which are principal bundle isomorphisms, therefore $\psi_a(p_a g_a) = \psi_a(p_a) g_a$, where the action of $G_a$ on $U_i \times G_a$ is given by $(x, g_a) g'_a = (x, g_a g'_a)$. From this follows that $F_i(p_1 g_1) = F_i(p_1) g_1$. On the other hand, for $p_1 \in \pi^{-1}(U_{ij})$ we have $F_i(p_1) = F_j(p_1)$. Indeed, we have the commutative diagram for $a = 1, 2$: \begin{equation} \xymatrix{ U_{ij} \times G_a{}\ar[rr]^{(x, g_a) \to (x, g^a_{ji} g_a)} & & U_{ij} \times G_a \\ &\pi_1^{-1}(U_{ij}) \ar[lu]^{\psi^a_i} \ar[ru]_{\psi^a_j} & } \end{equation} Let $p_1 \in \pi^{-1}(U_{ij})$ and $\psi^1_i(p_1) = (x, g_1)$, then $\psi^1_j(p_1) = (x, g^1_{ji} g_1)$. Also $\psi^2_i F_i(p_1) = (x, f(g_1))$, hence $\psi^2_j F_i(p_1) = (x, g^2_{ji} f(g_1))$. Therefore, \begin{equation} \psi^2_j F_j(p_1) = (x, f(g^1_{ji} g_1)) = (x, f(g^1_{ji}) f(g_1)) = (x, g^2_{ji} f(g_1)) = \psi^2_j F_i(p_1), \end{equation} thus $F_j = F_i$ on $\pi^{-1}(U_{ij})$ and therefore $\left\{ F_i \right\}$ determine a homomorphism $F : P_1 \to P_2$. \end{proof} From the construction of the bundle $\widetilde{P}$ it follows that $P = \widetilde{P}/Z$ and the principal fiber bundle homomorphism constructed in Lemma~\ref{lm:2} is exactly the projection $\widetilde{P} \to P=\widetilde{P}/Z$.
nodes.statement_short: Direct cocycle computation with the lifted transition functions, then rebuild $\widetilde P$ from a coboundary and invoke the transition-function lemma.

nodes.name: $z$ is a normalized cochain
nodes.statement: Let us prove that $\left\{ z_{ijk} \right\}$ is a \v Chech cocycle on $\mathcal{U}$. First of all note that we have \begin{equation} \widetilde{g}_{ij} \widetilde{g}_{jk} = z_{ijk} \widetilde{g}_{ik} = \widetilde{g}_{ik} z_{ijk}. \end{equation} Then \begin{equation} (\widetilde{g}_{ij} \widetilde{g}_{jk}) \widetilde{g}_{ki} = z_{ijk} \widetilde{g}_{ik} \widetilde{g}_{ki} = z_{ijk} \text{ and } \widetilde{g}_{ij} (\widetilde{g}_{jk} \widetilde{g}_{ki}) = \widetilde{g}_{ij} \widetilde{g}_{ji} z_{jki} = z_{jki}, \end{equation} therefore $z_{ijk} = z_{kij} = z_{jki}$. At the same time, \begin{equation} z_{ijk}^{-1} \widetilde{g}_{ik}^{-1} = \left( z_{ijk} \widetilde{g}_{ik} \right)^{-1} = \left( \widetilde{g}_{ij} \widetilde{g}_{jk} \right)^{-1} = \widetilde{g}_{kj} \widetilde{g}_{ji} = z_{kji} \widetilde{g}_{ki}, \end{equation} hence follows that $z_{ijk}^{-1} = z_{kji} = z_{jik}$. Moreover $z_{ijk} = 1$ if at least two indices coincide. Thus $z = \left\{ z_{ijk} \right\}$ is a normalized cochain.
nodes.statement_short: Index symmetries and $z_{ijk}=1$ on repeated indices give normalization.

nodes.name: $z$ is a cocycle: $\delta z = 0$
nodes.statement: Now we have \begin{equation} (\widetilde{g}_{ij} \widetilde{g}_{jk}) (\widetilde{g}_{kj} \widetilde{g}_{jl}) = z_{ijk} \widetilde{g}_{ik} z_{kjl} \widetilde{g}_{kl} = z_{ijk} z_{kjl} z_{ikl} g_{il} \end{equation} and \begin{equation} (\widetilde{g}_{ij} \widetilde{g}_{jk}) (\widetilde{g}_{kj} \widetilde{g}_{jl}) = (\widetilde{g}_{ij} (\widetilde{g}_{jk} (\widetilde{g}_{kj}) \widetilde{g}_{jl} = \widetilde{g}_{ij} \widetilde{g}_{jl} = z_{ijl} \widetilde{g}_{il}, \end{equation} thus $z_{ijk} z_{kjl} z_{ikl} = z_{ijl}$, this implies \begin{equation} \delta z = z_{jkl} z_{ikl}^{-1} z_{ijl} z_{ijk}^{-1} = 0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Associativity of the lifted products yields $z_{ijk}z_{kjl}z_{ikl}=z_{ijl}$, i.e. $\delta z=0$.

nodes.name: Coboundary case: construct $\widetilde{P}$
nodes.statement: If $z = \delta u$, where $u = \left\{ u_{ij} \in Z \right\}$, then \begin{equation} z_{ijk} = u_{ij} u_{jk} u_{ki}. \end{equation} Therefore we can construct the $\widetilde{G}$-principal bundle $\widetilde{P} \to M$ with the transition functions $\widetilde{g}'_{ij} = \widetilde{g}_{ij} u_{ji}$ because \begin{equation} \widetilde{g}'_{ij} \widetilde{g}'_{jk} \widetilde{g}'_{ki} =\widetilde{g}_{ij} u_{ji} \widetilde{g}_{jk} u_{kj} \widetilde{g}_{ki} u_{ik} =\widetilde{g}_{ij} \widetilde{g}_{jk} \widetilde{g}_{ki} u_{ji} u_{kj} u_{ik} = z_{ijk} u_{ji} u_{kj} u_{ik} = 1. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: If $z=\delta u$, the corrected functions $\widetilde g'_{ij}=\widetilde g_{ij}u_{ji}$ satisfy the cocycle condition and define $\widetilde P$.

nodes.name: Produce the bundle morphism via the lemma
nodes.statement: Now we have that $p(\widetilde{g}'_{ij}) = g_{ij}$ and from the following lemma it follows that there exists a principal bundle morphism $\pi : \widetilde{P} \to P$ written with respect to the trivializations as $(x, \widetilde{g}) \to (x, p(\widetilde{g}))$.
nodes.statement_short: Since $p(\widetilde g'_{ij})=g_{ij}$, the transition-function lemma gives a morphism $\widetilde P\to P$.

nodes.name: Conclude $P = \widetilde{P}/Z$
nodes.statement: From the construction of the bundle $\widetilde{P}$ it follows that $P = \widetilde{P}/Z$ and the principal fiber bundle homomorphism constructed in Lemma~\ref{lm:2} is exactly the projection $\widetilde{P} \to P=\widetilde{P}/Z$.
nodes.statement_short: The morphism is the quotient projection, so $P\cong\widetilde P/Z$.

nodes.name: Principal bundle homomorphism from matching transition functions
nodes.statement: Let $G_a$, $a = 1, 2$ be Lie groups. Let $\pi_a : P_a \to M$, $a = 1, 2$ be a $G_a$-principal bundle and $f : G_1 \to G_2$ be a Lie group homomorphism. Assume that $\mathcal{U} = \left\{ U_i \right\}$ is a trivializing covering for $P_1$ and $P_2$ at the same time. If the transition functions $g^a_{ij}$ with respect to the covering $\mathcal{U}$ are related by $f(g^1_{ij}) = g^2_{ij}$, then there exists a principal fiber bundle homomorphism $F : P_1 \to P_2$ corresponding to $f$, i.\, e. $F(p_1 g_1) = F(p_1) f(g_1)$.
nodes.statement_short: If transition functions correspond under a Lie group homomorphism $f$, the bundles are related by an $f$-equivariant bundle morphism.
assumptions: Let $G_a$, $a = 1, 2$ be Lie groups.
Let $\pi_a : P_a \to M$, $a = 1, 2$ be a $G_a$-principal bundle and $f : G_1 \to G_2$ be a Lie group homomorphism.
Assume that $\mathcal{U} = \left\{ U_i \right\}$ is a trivializing covering for $P_1$ and $P_2$ at the same time.
If the transition functions $g^a_{ij}$ with respect to the covering $\mathcal{U}$ are related by $f(g^1_{ij}) = g^2_{ij}$
conclusions: then there exists a principal fiber bundle homomorphism $F : P_1 \to P_2$ corresponding to $f$, i.\, e. $F(p_1 g_1) = F(p_1) f(g_1)$.

nodes.name: Proof of the transition-function lemma
nodes.statement: We define $F_i : \pi_1^{-1}(U_i) \to \pi_2^{-1}(U_i)$ by the commutative diagram \begin{equation} \xymatrix{ \pi_1^{-1}(U_i) \ar[r]^{F_i} \ar[d]_{\psi_i^1} & \pi_2^{-1}(U_i) \ar[d]^{\psi_i^2} \\ U_i \times G_1 \ar[r]^{ 1 \times f} & U_i \times G_2 } \end{equation} where $\psi_a$ are the trivializations which are principal bundle isomorphisms, therefore $\psi_a(p_a g_a) = \psi_a(p_a) g_a$, where the action of $G_a$ on $U_i \times G_a$ is given by $(x, g_a) g'_a = (x, g_a g'_a)$. From this follows that $F_i(p_1 g_1) = F_i(p_1) g_1$. On the other hand, for $p_1 \in \pi^{-1}(U_{ij})$ we have $F_i(p_1) = F_j(p_1)$. Indeed, we have the commutative diagram for $a = 1, 2$: \begin{equation} \xymatrix{ U_{ij} \times G_a{}\ar[rr]^{(x, g_a) \to (x, g^a_{ji} g_a)} & & U_{ij} \times G_a \\ &\pi_1^{-1}(U_{ij}) \ar[lu]^{\psi^a_i} \ar[ru]_{\psi^a_j} & } \end{equation} Let $p_1 \in \pi^{-1}(U_{ij})$ and $\psi^1_i(p_1) = (x, g_1)$, then $\psi^1_j(p_1) = (x, g^1_{ji} g_1)$. Also $\psi^2_i F_i(p_1) = (x, f(g_1))$, hence $\psi^2_j F_i(p_1) = (x, g^2_{ji} f(g_1))$. Therefore, \begin{equation} \psi^2_j F_j(p_1) = (x, f(g^1_{ji} g_1)) = (x, f(g^1_{ji}) f(g_1)) = (x, g^2_{ji} f(g_1)) = \psi^2_j F_i(p_1), \end{equation} thus $F_j = F_i$ on $\pi^{-1}(U_{ij})$ and therefore $\left\{ F_i \right\}$ determine a homomorphism $F : P_1 \to P_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $F$ chartwise through the trivializations and check the local definitions agree on overlaps.

nodes.name: Define $F_i$ chartwise and check equivariance
nodes.statement: We define $F_i : \pi_1^{-1}(U_i) \to \pi_2^{-1}(U_i)$ by the commutative diagram \begin{equation} \xymatrix{ \pi_1^{-1}(U_i) \ar[r]^{F_i} \ar[d]_{\psi_i^1} & \pi_2^{-1}(U_i) \ar[d]^{\psi_i^2} \\ U_i \times G_1 \ar[r]^{ 1 \times f} & U_i \times G_2 } \end{equation} where $\psi_a$ are the trivializations which are principal bundle isomorphisms, therefore $\psi_a(p_a g_a) = \psi_a(p_a) g_a$, where the action of $G_a$ on $U_i \times G_a$ is given by $(x, g_a) g'_a = (x, g_a g'_a)$. From this follows that $F_i(p_1 g_1) = F_i(p_1) g_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Build $F_i$ from the trivializations and $1\times f$; equivariance is inherited.

nodes.name: Check agreement on overlaps
nodes.statement: On the other hand, for $p_1 \in \pi^{-1}(U_{ij})$ we have $F_i(p_1) = F_j(p_1)$. Indeed, we have the commutative diagram for $a = 1, 2$: \begin{equation} \xymatrix{ U_{ij} \times G_a{}\ar[rr]^{(x, g_a) \to (x, g^a_{ji} g_a)} & & U_{ij} \times G_a \\ &\pi_1^{-1}(U_{ij}) \ar[lu]^{\psi^a_i} \ar[ru]_{\psi^a_j} & } \end{equation} Let $p_1 \in \pi^{-1}(U_{ij})$ and $\psi^1_i(p_1) = (x, g_1)$, then $\psi^1_j(p_1) = (x, g^1_{ji} g_1)$. Also $\psi^2_i F_i(p_1) = (x, f(g_1))$, hence $\psi^2_j F_i(p_1) = (x, g^2_{ji} f(g_1))$. Therefore, \begin{equation} \psi^2_j F_j(p_1) = (x, f(g^1_{ji} g_1)) = (x, f(g^1_{ji}) f(g_1)) = (x, g^2_{ji} f(g_1)) = \psi^2_j F_i(p_1), \end{equation} thus $F_j = F_i$ on $\pi^{-1}(U_{ij})$ and therefore $\left\{ F_i \right\}$ determine a homomorphism $F : P_1 \to P_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Compatibility $f(g^1_{ji})=g^2_{ji}$ makes $F_i=F_j$ on overlaps, so the $F_i$ glue.

nodes.name: Obstruction class for a projective bundle of odd rank
nodes.statement: If $Q \to M$ is a projective bundle of odd rank $n$ and is oriented, then the obstruction to existence of a vector bundle $E$ such that $Q = P(E)$ is an element in $H^2(M, \mathbb{Z}_2)$.
assumptions: If $Q \to M$ is a projective bundle of odd rank $n$ and is oriented
conclusions: then the obstruction to existence of a vector bundle $E$ such that $Q = P(E)$ is an element in $H^2(M, \mathbb{Z}_2)$.

nodes.name: bundle of projective frames
nodes.statement: Let $Q \to M$ be a projective bundle of rank $n$. The principal bundle $PGL(Q)$ with the group $PGL(n)$ adjoint to $Q$ is called the \emph{bundle of projective frames}.
nodes.genus: The principal bundle $PGL(Q)$ with the group $PGL(n)$ adjoint to $Q$

nodes.name: $PGL(Q)$ as a quotient of the linear frame bundle
nodes.statement: On the total space of a vector bundle $E \to M$ the group $\mathbb{R}^{*} = \mathbb{R} \setminus \left\{ 0 \right\}$ acts freely by scaling, and $Q = P(E)$ is the quotient of $E$ with respect to this action. Therefore, we have the $\mathbb{R}^{*}$-principal bundle $\pi : E \to Q$. Also we have the induced action of $\mathbb{R}^{*}$ on the total space of the linear frame bundle $GL(E)$, and the quotient space is $PGL(Q)$. The quotient map $GL(E) \to PGL(Q)$ is $\mathbb{R}^{*}$-principal bundle. If $E$ is an orientable vector bundle of rank $n + 1$, where $n$ is odd, then the structure group $GL(n + 1)$ of $GL(E)$ reduces to $SL(n + 1)$, and in this case we have the double covering $SL(E) \to PGL(Q)$. For an orientable vector bundle $E$ of rank $n + 1$, one can take a metric $g$ on $E$, therefore the $GL(n + 1)$-principal bundle $GL(E)$ of linear frames reduces to a $SO(n + 1)$-principal bundle of positively oriented orthonormal frames $SO(E)$. Therefore, for $Q = P(E)$, the bundle $PGL(Q)$ reduces to the subgroup $SO(n + 1)/{\pm I} \subset PGL(n) = SL(n + 1)/{\pm I}$.

nodes.name: projective connection
nodes.statement: Let $Q \to M$ be a projective bundle. A projective connection is a connection in $PGL(Q)$.

nodes.name: When two linear connections induce the same projective connection
nodes.statement:
Two linear connections $
abla$ and $
abla'$ in the vector bundle $E$ induce the same projective connection in $P(E)$ if and only if the deformation tensor $T = 
abla' - 
abla$ has the form  egin{equation} T_i{}^a_b = \xi_i \delta^a_b. \end{equation}

conclusions: induce the same projective connection in $P(E)$ if and only if the deformation tensor $T = \nabla' - \nabla$ has the form
T_i{}^a_b = \xi_i \delta^a_b.

nodes.name: Equi-affine connections correspond to projective connections
nodes.statement: Let $E$ be an oriented vector bundle, and $\theta \in \Omega^{n + 1}E$ be a volume form in $E$. Then there is one-to-one correspondence between equi-affine connections on $E$ with respect to $\theta$ and the projective connections in $P(E)$.
assumptions: Let $E$ be an oriented vector bundle, and $\theta \in \Omega^{n + 1}E$ be a volume form in $E$.
conclusions: Then there is one-to-one correspondence between equi-affine connections on $E$ with respect to $\theta$ and the projective connections in $P(E)$.

nodes.name: The correspondence in terms of parallel translation
nodes.statement:
In terms of parallel translation this correspondence can be explained as follows. Let $\Gamma$ be a projective connection in $Q = P(E)$ induced by a linear connection $
abla$ in $E$. In terms of the parallel translation this means that a section $L$ of $Q$ along $\gamma$ is parallel with respect to the connection $\Gamma$ if there exists a section $s$ of $E$ along $\gamma$ which is parallel with respect to $
abla$ and generates $L$. This can be expressed also in terms of covariant derivative: $L = [ s ]$ is parallel with respect to $\Gamma$ if and only if $
abla_{\dot\gamma} s = \mu s$. Now any projective frame field $\mathcal{L} = \left\{ L_0, L_1, \cdots, L_n ight\}$ in $Q = P(E)$ determines a frame field $\mathcal{E} = \left\{E_1, \cdots, E_night\}$ in $E$ such that $L_i = [ E_i ]$, and $L_0 = [ E_0 ]$, where $E_0 = E_1 + E_2 + \cdots + E_n$, up to a scaling. If in addition we have a volume form $	heta$, the projective frame field determines the linear frame field $\left\{ E_i ight\}$ up to a sign. Then $
abla_{\dot\gamma} E_i = \mu_i E_i$ and $
abla_{\dot\gamma} E_0 = \mu_0 E_0$, hence follows that $\mu_0 = \mu_1 = \cdots = \mu_n$. If we assume that the linear connection $
abla$ is equi-affine with respect to a volume form $	heta$, then $
abla 	heta = 0$ and the function $\mu_0 =  rac{d}{dt} \log 	heta(E_1, \cdots, E_n)$.

nodes.name: Sections of a rank-$1$ projective bundle and $Aff(1)$-reductions
nodes.statement: Let $Q$ be a projective bundle of rank $1$. Let $Aff(1) \subset PGL(1)$ be the subgroup of affine transformations of line. Then $Q \cong PGL(Q)/Aff(1)$ and a section of projective bundle $Q$ is equivalent to the reduction of the bundle $PGL(Q)$ to the subgroup $Aff(1)$.
assumptions: Let $Q$ be a projective bundle of rank $1$.
Let $Aff(1) \subset PGL(1)$ be the subgroup of affine transformations of line.
conclusions: Then $Q \cong PGL(Q)/Aff(1)$ and a section of projective bundle $Q$ is equivalent to the reduction of the bundle $PGL(Q)$ to the subgroup $Aff(1)$.

nodes.name: Proof via transitivity of $PGL(1)$ on $\mathbb{R}P^1$
nodes.statement: This follows from the fact that the group $PGL(1)$ acts transitively on $\mathbb{R}P^1$, and the isotropy subgroup of a point in $\mathbb{R}P^1$ is the group $Aff(1)$.
nodes.statement_short: Identify $\mathbb{R}P^1$ as the homogeneous space $PGL(1)/Aff(1)$ by transitivity and isotropy.

nodes.name: The half-angular form $\theta$ on $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{0\}$
nodes.statement: Let us consider the form \begin{equation} \theta = \frac{1}{2} \frac{1}{(v^1)^2 + (v^2)^2} \left(-v^2 dv^1 + v^1 dv^2\right) \in \Omega^1(\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \left\{ 0 \right\}), \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Half the angular form on the punctured plane; it descends to a generator $\bar\alpha$ of $H^1(\mathbb{R}P^1)$.

nodes.name: Exterior derivative of the covariant coframe $Dy^a$
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} d(Dy^a) = \Gamma_i{ }^a_b Dy^b \wedge dx^i + R_{ij}{ }^a_b y^b dx^i \wedge dx^j, \end{equation} where $R_{ij}{ }^a_b = \partial_i \Gamma_j{ }^a_b - \partial_j \Gamma_i{ }^a_b + \Gamma_i{ }^a_c \Gamma_j{}^c_b - \Gamma_j{ }^a_c \Gamma_i{}^c_b$ is the curvature tensor of the linear connection in $E$.
nodes.statement_short: $d(Dy^a)$ splits into a connection term and a curvature term $R_{ij}{}^a_b y^b dx^i\wedge dx^j$.
assumptions: Consider the local coframe $dx^i$, $Dy^a = dy^a + \Gamma_i{ }^a_b y^b dx^i$.
conclusions: d(Dy^a) = \Gamma_i{ }^a_b Dy^b \wedge dx^i + R_{ij}{ }^a_b y^b dx^i \wedge dx^j,

nodes.name: Proof of the derivative formula for $Dy^a$
nodes.statement: We have \begin{multline} d(Dy^a) =d( dy^a + \Gamma_i{ }^a_b y^b dx^i ) =d\Gamma_i{ }^a_b y^b \wedge dx^i + \Gamma_i{ }^a_b dy^b \wedge dx^i = \\ \partial_j\Gamma_i{ }^a_b y^b dx^j \wedge dx^i + \Gamma_i{ }^a_b (Dy^b - \Gamma_j{}^b_c y^c dx^j) \wedge dx^i = \\ \Gamma_i{ }^a_b Dy^b \wedge dx^i + \left(\partial_j\Gamma_i{ }^a_b y^b dx^j \wedge dx^i - \Gamma_i{ }^a_b \Gamma_j{}^b_c y^c dx^j \wedge dx^i \right) = \\ \Gamma_i{ }^a_b Dy^b \wedge dx^i + \left(\partial_j\Gamma_i{ }^a_b y^b dx^j \wedge dx^i + \Gamma_j{ }^a_b \Gamma_i{}^b_c y^c dx^j \wedge dx^i \right) = \\ \Gamma_i{ }^a_b Dy^b \wedge dx^i + R_{ij}{ }^a_b y^b dx^i \wedge dx^j. \end{multline}
nodes.statement_short: Direct differentiation of $Dy^a=dy^a+\Gamma_i{}^a_b y^b dx^i$ and regrouping into the curvature tensor.

nodes.name: The vertical form on a projectivized vector bundle
nodes.statement: Let $E \to M$ be a vector bundle, $Q = P(E)$, and $j : P(E) \to Q$. \begin{enumerate} \item There exist a $1$-form $\alpha \in \Omega^1(Q)$ such that $\hat{\alpha} = j^* \alpha$. \item $\left.\alpha\right|_H = 0$ \item $d i_x \alpha = 0$, and $i_x^*\alpha$ represents the class $[\bar \alpha] \in H^1(\mathbb{R}P^1)$. \item $d\alpha = \frac{1}{2} \pi^*(\Omega)$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: $\hat\alpha$ descends to a form $\alpha$ on $Q=P(E)$ which is vertical, represents the generator of $H^1(\mathbb{R}P^1)$, and has $d\alpha=\tfrac12\pi^*\Omega$.
assumptions: Let $E \to M$ be a vector bundle, $Q = P(E)$, and $j : P(E) \to Q$.
conclusions: There exist a $1$-form $\alpha \in \Omega^1(Q)$ such that $\hat{\alpha} = j^* \alpha$.
